sections.h2: How does unpaid Ohio property tax become a lien?
sections.html:
It is a lien from the first day of each tax year. R.C. 323.11 says the state's lien for the real property tax attaches on January 1 and continues until the tax, penalties, interest and charges are paid. The bill does not arrive until later, but the claim on the parcel already exists.

The lien is why an unpaid balance cannot be left behind at a closing. If only part of a tract is transferred, the same section allows the tax to be apportioned, and the lien then reaches each part only up to the amount allocated to it.

The county treasurer, through the prosecuting attorney, files the foreclosure case, and the owner gets several chances to pay before the property is sold.

sections.h2: When does an Ohio county start tax foreclosure?
sections.html:
The treasurer may sue once taxes remain unpaid for sixty days after the delinquent land duplicate is delivered to the treasurer. R.C. 323.25 lets the treasurer enforce the lien by civil action the way a mortgage is foreclosed, in the common pleas court, in a municipal court with jurisdiction, or before the county Board of Revision where that board has authority.

A second route sits in R.C. 5721.18. The prosecuting attorney files in the name of the treasurer once the auditor delivers the delinquent land certificate or master list. An in rem action, one against the parcel itself, may be filed after the end of the second year from the date the delinquency was first certified.

The treasurer cannot enforce the lien while any of these applies:

  • The parcel is the subject of a pending application for exemption and is not on the delinquent land duplicate.
  • A valid delinquent tax contract is in force and has not been voided.
  • A tax certificate on the parcel has been sold, as to the taxes it covers.

sections.h2: What can I do to stop a tax foreclosure in Ohio?
sections.html:
Pay the delinquency, or arrange a plan. R.C. 323.31 entitles an owner who lives in the home, or a land contract buyer who occupies it, to at least one written delinquent tax contract with the treasurer, so long as no tax lien certificate or foreclosure judgment is outstanding. Residential contracts last up to five years, and at least two years if the owner asks. Later contracts are at the treasurer's discretion.

The statute lets the contract be signed any time before the adjudication of foreclosure. It breaks if an installment is missed or the current taxes go unpaid, and the prosecuting attorney then files the foreclosure. If a tax certificate was sold, the owner uses a redemption payment plan under section 5721.38 instead.

The right to redeem stays open for a while after suit is filed. R.C. 5721.25 lets any person entitled to redeem pay the taxes, assessments, penalties, interest, charges and costs to the treasurer before foreclosure starts. After filing, redemption is still possible until the entry confirming the sale, or until the alternative redemption period ends, but the owner must also show the property meets zoning, land use, building, health and safety codes. A delinquent tax contract can even be signed after filing, up to five years, though the case keeps moving and the contract can end if the property falls out of code compliance.

sections.h2: What is the alternative redemption period and abandoned land?
sections.html:
It is a short window after judgment. R.C. 323.65 defines it as twenty-eight days after the adjudication of foreclosure is journalized, ending on and including the twenty-eighth day. When it expires, the owner's right and equity of redemption end without a further order. A county treasurer chooses whether to invoke it under section 323.78.

If it is invoked and a city, township, county, school district, community development organization or land reutilization corporation has asked for the parcel, the court or board orders the property deeded to that body without appraisal or sale, free of the taxes and other liens. If nobody asked, the parcel is sold as usual, and if no one bids it is forfeited to the state.

The expedited process for abandoned land is built on the word unoccupied. The statute treats a parcel as unoccupied when no taxable building is lived in, no trade or business is active there, or the parcel is uninhabited with no sign of a change of tenants or improvements. A presumption arises if the parcel is not agricultural and at least two of these hold at certification:

  • No person, trade or business is visibly present at an exterior inspection by the county, municipality or township.
  • No utility connections serve it, or none are being billed.
  • It is boarded up or sealed after being found open, vacant or vandalized.
  • It is insecure, vacant or vandalized on visible inspection.

sections.h2: How do the stages compare, and what happens at the tax sale?
sections.html:
The table lines up the main stages of a county tax foreclosure.

Stages of Ohio delinquent land tax enforcement
StageKey ruleSection
Lien attachesJanuary 1 of each tax year323.11
Suit by treasurerAfter 60 days from delivery of delinquent duplicate323.25
Answer in an in rem actionWithin 28 days after service is complete5721.18
Payment planUp to 5 years for an owner-occupied home323.31
Alternative redemption28 days after judgment is journalized323.65
Second sale if no bidNot less than 2 or more than 6 weeks later5721.19

In an in rem case the answer deadline matters most: section 5721.18 says a default judgment may be taken on any parcel without an answer, and it binds everyone with an interest in it, including those out of state.

Under R.C. 5721.19, the court may order a parcel sold without appraisal for not less than the lesser of two figures: the auditor's fair market value plus costs, or the total amount found due plus costs. If no bid reaches that figure, the sale is adjourned to a second date. If a sale brings less than what is owed, the court may enter a deficiency judgment against the owner of record. A sale in an in rem case under division (B) leaves the buyer with title free of most liens, apart from a properly filed federal tax lien and earlier easements and covenants.

sections.h2: What if I sell the house or money is left after the sale?
sections.html:
Selling does not end a case already filed. R.C. 5721.18(D) says a conveyance after the complaint is filed, and before the foreclosure judgment, does not nullify the county's right to proceed. Ask the treasurer and the prosecuting attorney for a payoff figure that includes the costs of the case, have it paid from the proceeds at closing, and get written confirmation that the case is resolved.

A sale of land for delinquent taxes carries no auditor's conveyance fee under R.C. 319.54, which lists transfers on sale for delinquent taxes among its exemptions.

When a foreclosure sale brings more than the judgment, R.C. 5721.20 sends the excess to the clerk of court within forty-five days after confirmation. The clerk notifies the owner. If the owner does not claim it within ninety days of the final notice, it goes to the county treasury, where the treasurer holds it for three years. After that it is forfeited to the delinquent tax and assessment collection fund, or to a land reutilization fund where the county has one.

faqs.q: How long can I be behind on Ohio property tax before foreclosure?
faqs.a: The treasurer may sue sixty days after the delinquent land duplicate is delivered. A prosecuting attorney in rem action can follow after the second year from first certification. Ask the treasurer where your parcel stands.

faqs.q: Can I set up a payment plan for delinquent Ohio taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. An owner who lives in the home is entitled to at least one delinquent tax contract, up to five years, or two if requested. No tax lien certificate or foreclosure judgment can be outstanding when the first contract is signed.

faqs.q: Can I still pay after the county files a tax foreclosure?
faqs.a: Yes. You can redeem by paying everything due plus costs before the entry confirming the sale, or before the alternative redemption period of twenty-eight days after judgment ends. The property must also meet local building and zoning codes.

faqs.q: What does the alternative redemption period mean?
faqs.a: It is the twenty-eight days after the court or Board of Revision journalizes the foreclosure judgment. When it ends, the owner's right of redemption is over with no further order. Only counties whose treasurer invokes it use it.

faqs.q: Do I get money back if my house sells for more than the taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes, excess proceeds go to the clerk, who notifies the owner. If it is unclaimed within ninety days of the final notice, it is held by the county treasurer, and the owner may demand it within three years.
